analysis.investment_thesis: Neogen is a capital-hungry specialty chemicals business drowning in debt and priced at 150x earnings despite a 5.59% ROE and six consecutive years of negative free cash flow. The business is destroying capital, not creating it — the antithesis of what I look for.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of 25.6% over 9 years shows genuine demand for bromine/lithium chemistry products
Exports to 33 countries with diversified end-markets including battery materials — a real secular growth vector
Gross margin of 45.85% suggests some pricing power at the product level
key_risks: Debt explosion: borrowings surged from 409 Cr (FY24) to 1,132 Cr (FY25), pushing D/E to 1.41 — in a cyclical, capital-intensive business, this is dangerous
Finance costs (48 Cr) nearly equal net profit (35 Cr) and are growing at 28.6% CAGR — interest burden is structurally eroding earnings
FCF has been negative every single year since at least FY20 (cumulative ~-766 Cr), with 318 Cr capex in FY25 and 335 Cr CWIP still to be absorbed
red_flags: ROE of 5.59% is less than a fixed deposit — the business earns far below its cost of capital
Net profit stagnated/declined: 50 Cr → 36 Cr → 35 Cr (FY23-25) while revenue grew — profits are being swallowed by interest and capex depreciation
P/E of 150x (forward 65.8x) for a company with declining earnings and 1.41 D/E offers zero margin of safety
Other income turned sharply negative (-10 Cr in FY25) after masking weak core earnings in prior years
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Neogen fails my most basic tests. I demand a durable competitive advantage translated into high returns on equity — Neogen delivers 5.59% ROE. That means for every 100 rupees of shareholder capital employed, the business earns less than 6 rupees. Meanwhile, it has taken on debt at rates that cost it 48 Cr in interest on a business earning only 35 Cr in net profit. The finance cost CAGR of 28.6% is outrunning revenue growth of 25.6%, and the company's net profit has been flat-to-declining for three years while the balance sheet nearly doubled. This is the opposite of a self-funding compounding machine.

The capex story — 303 Cr in FY24, 318 Cr in FY25, and 335 Cr still sitting in CWIP — is the bull case, but it requires massive faith: faith that these assets will generate adequate returns, faith that debt can be serviced and refinanced, and faith that specialty chemical pricing holds up. At 150x trailing P/E and EV/EBITDA of 39x, the market is pricing in perfection. I don't pay for hope. A business that has never generated positive free cash flow over a sustained period, funded by debt that now exceeds total equity, trading at one of the most extreme valuations I've seen — I would not touch this at any price remotely near current levels.
